draft.title: Transfer payments
card: A transfer payment is money the government pays to people who need support. The person pays nothing back and does not provide a good or service in return.
Examples in Australia are the Age Pension, Youth Allowance and JobSeeker Payment. Each is paid to people in a particular situation, such as older age, study or looking for work.
Payments are usually paid for from taxes. Money moves from the government's budget to households, so those households have more income to spend.
Many payments are means tested. This means a person with a higher income or more assets may get a smaller payment or none. This aims to direct help to people who need it most.
draft.remember: Transfer payments move money from the government to people who need support, with nothing provided in return.

a.q: Which of these is a transfer payment?
opts: The Age Pension paid to a retired person
Wages paid to a nurse in a public hospital
Interest paid on a bank savings account
A fee paid to a tutor for maths lessons
a.why: The Age Pension is money the government pays to a person who needs support, with no work or product given in return. Wages for a public hospital nurse come from the government too, but they are payment for work, so they are not a transfer payment.
a.clue: Which payment is made with nothing supplied in return?

b.q: Liam is 19 and studies full time. He gets Youth Allowance from the government. Why is this a transfer payment?
opts: He receives government money without providing work for it
He pays tax on it, so the money goes back to the government
He earns it by studying, which is a service to the government
It is paid by his university for the courses he completes
b.why: Youth Allowance is government money paid to a person who needs support, and Liam does not provide a good or service in return. Studying may be required to qualify, but it is not work sold to the government, so it does not make the payment a wage.
b.clue: Is the government buying anything from Liam?
